To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the LV pressure‐volume loop during PAP elevation is characterized by a distinct pattern of changes that can be described by a single equation.
the acute LV response to PAP elevation can be described by a pattern of LV pressure and volume changes, which allows calculation of Ees and PRWS.

(1) PAP‐derived PRSW was higher than vascular occlusion‐derived PRSW; (2) Ees derived from PAP‐related LV pressure and volume changes was lower than vascular occlusion–derived Ees; and (3) PAP‐related Ees and PRWS were significantly correlated with their vascular occlusion–based equivalents.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of PAP on LV function.
the LV pressure–volume response to PAP and the relationship of this response to vascular occlusion.
the LV response to increased intrathoracic pressure during mechanical ventilation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Ees and PRWS can be calculated from LV pressure–volume loops during positive pressure ventilation and that these values correlate with values derived during vascular occlusion.
the immediate LV response during the institution of PAP is a complex event that can be quantified and described in terms of systolic and diastolic function.

the LV pressure and volume response to acute PAP elevation can be described as a momentary pressure–volume loop that is consistent with a Frank–Starling mechanism, and that this momentary loop can be used to derive parameters of LV systolic function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the immediate LV pressure–volume response to increased airway pressure can be quantified and that these measurements can be used as surrogates for vascular occlusion measurements of LV systolic function.
the immediate LV response during institution of PAPP is a systematic event and can be described as a series of momentary events.
we have developed a new method for estimating systolic function during positive pressure ventilation, which is not dependent on vascular occlusion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the acute LV response to PAP elevation can be used to derive Ees and PRWS in the same way as with vascular occlusion.
Ees and PRWS can be derived from the LV pressure and volume response to airway inflation.
PAP‐derived PRSW is a better index of LV contractility than Ees, which is a function of the LV afterload.
